## Introduction

This document adopts the same workflow for analyzing urban phenology data, with the key modification of **replacing the climate variable with Daymet data**. The aim is to provide a basis for discussion with collaborators regarding the advantages and limitations of using Daymet data compared to Weather Underground (WU) data in urban phenology studies. In addition, this analysis seeks to explore how the choice of climate dataset (Daymet vs. WU) may influence the results and interpretations related to phenological patterns.

In brief, the goal of this analysis is to understand how temperature heterogeneity within the city influences phenological events, such as the start of season (SOS) and end of season (EOS), for various tree genera and species in urban environments. To achieve this, I apply spatial statistical models as described below:

$$y(\mathbf{s}_i, \mathbf{t}) = \mathbf{X}_{\mathbf{s}_i,\mathbf{t}} \boldsymbol{\beta} + w(\mathbf{s}_i) + u(\mathbf{t}) + \epsilon(\mathbf{s}_i, \mathbf{t})$$

where $y(\mathbf{s}_i, \mathbf{t})$ represents the phenological event (e.g., SOS or EOS) at location $\mathbf{s}_i$ and time $\mathbf{t}$.$\mathbf{X}_{\mathbf{s}_i,\mathbf{t}} = [1, \text{AvgTemp}_{\mathbf{s}_i,\mathbf{t}}, \text{Precp}_{\mathbf{s}_i,\mathbf{t}}, \text{srad}_{\mathbf{s}_i,\mathbf{t}}]$ is the design matrix of predictors. $\boldsymbol{\beta} = [\beta_0, \beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3]$ are the regression coefficients for the intercept and covariates. $\beta_1$ is the coefficient for the average temperature, which is the main interest in this study. The spatial random effect $w(\mathbf{s}_i)$ accounts for spatial autocorrelation among locations, while the temporal random effect $u(\mathbf{t})$ captures random year effect. Finally, $\epsilon(\mathbf{s}_i, \mathbf{t})$ represents the residual error term.

The analysis focuses on two main levels: genus and species, with particular attention to the city of New York.

## Data source comparison

Weather Underground (WU) data were obtained from the [Weather Underground program](https://www.wunderground.com/), drawing on multiple personal weather stations located within New York City. These data include daily measurements of temperature and precipitation. For the analysis, trees located within a 500 m buffer around the WU stations were selected.

Daymet data were accessed via the [Daymet](https://daymet.ornl.gov/), which provides gridded daily weather data at a spatial resolution of 1 km². For this comparison, I extracted daily maximum and minimum temperature as well as precipitation data for the same period (2016–2023). Given the full spatial coverage of Daymet, I conducted analyses for two sets of samples: (1) trees within a 500 m buffer of the WU sites and (2) all available trees across the city.

The figure below illustrates the direct comparison between the two datasets, focusing on the average seasonal temperature for trees within the WU buffer. The left panel shows the average winter temperature for the start of season (SOS) and the right panel displays the average summer temperature for the end of season (EOS). The x-axis represents the temperature from the WU data, while the y-axis represents the corresponding Daymet data. The red line represents a 1:1 relationship, indicating where the two datasets align perfectly.

```{r}
#| label: fig-compare-data
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-cap: "The comparison of temperature data from Weather Underground (WU) and Daymet for trees within the WU buffer in New York City"
#| warning: false
#| eval: true

source("~/phenology-urban/script/spatial_stats_model/tidy_data.R")
# compare 2 temp/prcp
valid_WU_Daymet <- readRDS("~/phenology-urban/data/proc/urban/NY/valid_WU_Daymet.rds")
wu_daymet_winter <- ggplot(data = valid_climate(valid_WU_Daymet, "SOS")) +
  geom_point(aes(x = temp_winter, y = temp_d_winter), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Weather Underground", y = "Daymet") +
  ggtitle("Spring temperature for SOS") +
  theme_minimal()
wu_daymet_summer <- ggplot(data = valid_climate(valid_WU_Daymet, "EOS")) +
  geom_point(aes(x = temp_summer, y = temp_d_summer), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Weather Underground", y = "Daymet") +
  ggtitle("Summer temperature for EOS") +
  theme_minimal()

wu_daymet_winter + wu_daymet_summer
```

Overall, the Daymet data show good alignment with the WU data. However, Daymet tends to report slightly lower temperatures than WU in both winter and summer (as indicated by most points falling below the 1:1 reference line). In winter, WU data exhibit a greater number of outliers, which may reflect the variability and less standardized measurement protocols of personal weather stations.

## Result (phenology response to temperature) comparison

In this section, I compare the results of spatial statistical models using WU data and Daymet data. The models are applied at both the genus and species levels, with a focus on the coefficients of the temperature variable in relation to 2 phenological events, the start of season (SOS) and end of season (EOS).

There are 3 sets of dataset and samples used:

1.  **WU data for trees within the WU buffer**: This set uses the WU data for trees located within a 500 m buffer around the WU stations ([@fig-genus-1] and [@fig-species-1]).
2.  **Daymet data for trees within the WU buffer**: This set uses the Daymet data for trees located within a 500 m buffer around the WU stations ([@fig-genus-2] and [@fig-species-2]).
3.  **Daymet data for all trees**: This set uses the Daymet data for all available trees across the city, regardless of their proximity to WU stations ([@fig-genus-3] and [@fig-species-3]).

Overall, the spatial statistical models using different data sources and sample sets show consistent patterns in the coefficients of the temperature variable. The temperature coefficients associated with SOS are generally positive, while those associated with EOS are generally negative. This indicates that higher temperatures are linked to an earlier start of season and a later end of season.

However, differences emerge in the magnitude and significance levels of the coefficients. In general, models using Daymet data tend to produce coefficients with larger magnitudes compared to those based on WU data for trees within the WU buffer. This may suggest that WU data capture greater variability in temperature — potentially reflecting more detailed intra-urban temperature differences, or possibly influenced by outliers in the personal weather station measurements.

### WU data for trees within the WU buffer

```{r data-1}
#| include: false
#| eval: false
points_in_buffer <- read_csv(paste0("~/phenology-urban/data/proc/urban/",city,"/tree_WU_500_buffer_PS.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  
  all_sites_temp <- readRDS(paste0("~/urban-cooling/data/raw/WU/",city,"/",city,"_wu.rds")) %>%
    dplyr::select(c(Date, HighTemp, AvgTemp, LowTemp, Sum_mm, name)) %>%
    mutate(season = case_when(
      month(Date) %in% 3:5 ~ "spring",
      month(Date) %in% 6:8 ~ "summer",
      month(Date) %in% 9:11 ~ "fall",
      month(Date) %in% c(12, 1, 2) ~ "winter"
    )) %>%
    mutate(year = year(Date),
           year = if_else(month(Date) == 12, year + 1, year)) %>%
    group_by(name, year, season) %>%
    summarise(
      Avg_AvgTemp = mean(AvgTemp, na.rm = TRUE),
      Sum_Sum_mm = sum(Sum_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
      AvgTemp_count = sum(!is.na(AvgTemp)),
      Sum_mm_count = sum(!is.na(Sum_mm)),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
  
  srad_daily <- readRDS(paste0("~/phenology-urban/data/raw/",city,"/Daymet/daily2016-2024/srad_daily_2016-2023.rds")) %>%
    select(id, value, date)  %>%
    mutate(season = case_when(
      month(date) %in% 3:5 ~ "spring",
      month(date) %in% 6:8 ~ "summer",
      month(date) %in% 9:11 ~ "fall",
      month(date) %in% c(12, 1, 2) ~ "winter"
    )) %>%
    mutate(year = year(date),
           year = if_else(month(date) == 12, year + 1, year)) %>%
    group_by(id, year, season) %>%
    summarise(
      Avg_srad = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
      srad_count = sum(!is.na(value)),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
```

### Daymet temperature and precipitation for trees within the WU buffer

```{r data-2}
#| eval: false
#| include: false

## prepare input data
points_in_buffer <- read_csv(paste0("~/phenology-urban/data/proc/urban/",city,"/tree_WU_500_buffer_PS.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

# List of variable names and their corresponding filenames
files <- c("tmax_monthly_WU_buffer.rds", "tmin_monthly_WU_buffer.rds", "prcp_monthly_WU_buffer.rds")
base_path <- "~/phenology-urban/data/raw/"
processed_data_list <- lapply(files, function(file_name) {
  # Read the file
  var_name <- sub("_monthly_WU_buffer.rds", "", file_name)
  data <- readRDS(paste0(base_path, city, "/Daymet/monthly2016-2024/", file_name)) %>%
    select(id, value, date) %>%
    mutate(
      season = case_when(
        substr(date, 6, 7) %in% c("03", "04", "05") ~ "spring",
        substr(date, 6, 7) %in% c("06", "07", "08") ~ "summer",
        substr(date, 6, 7) %in% c("09", "10", "11") ~ "fall",
        substr(date, 6, 7) %in% c("12", "01", "02") ~ "winter"
      )) %>%
    mutate(year = as.integer(substr(date, 1, 4)),
           year = if_else(substr(date, 6, 7) == "12", year + 1, year)) %>%
    group_by(id, year, season) %>%
    summarise(
    # Use sum for prcp, and mean for tmax and tmin
    Avg_value = ifelse(var_name == "prcp", sum(value, na.rm = TRUE), mean(value, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  # Rename the Avg_value column to the variable name (e.g., tmax, tmin, prcp)
  rename(!!var_name := Avg_value)
  
  return(data)
})

all_sites_temp_d <- processed_data_list[[1]]
for (i in 2:length(processed_data_list)) {
  all_sites_temp_d <- left_join(all_sites_temp_d, processed_data_list[[i]], by = c("id", "season", "year"))
}
  
srad_daily <- readRDS(paste0("~/phenology-urban/data/raw/",city,"/Daymet/daily2016-2024/srad_daily_2016-2023.rds")) %>%
  select(id, value, date)  %>%
  mutate(season = case_when(
    month(date) %in% 3:5 ~ "spring",
    month(date) %in% 6:8 ~ "summer",
    month(date) %in% 9:11 ~ "fall",
    month(date) %in% c(12, 1, 2) ~ "winter"
  )) %>%
  mutate(year = year(date),
         year = if_else(month(date) == 12, year + 1, year)) %>%
  group_by(id, year, season) %>%
  summarise(
    Avg_srad = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    srad_count = sum(!is.na(value)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

### Daymet temperature and precipitation for all available trees

```{r data-3}
#| eval: false
#| include: false
city <- "NY"

## prepare input data
metadata <- read_csv("~/lab-data/datasets/vegetation/PS/urban/metadata.csv") %>%
  filter(site == !!city)
file_list <- list.files(path = "~/lab-data/datasets/vegetation/PS/urban/doy", pattern = paste0("^doy_",city,"_.*\\.rds$"), full.names = TRUE)
data_list <- file_list %>%
  map(~ readRDS(.x))
all_doy <- bind_rows(data_list)
tree_location <- metadata %>%
  mutate(genus = str_extract(taxa, "^[^ ]+")) %>%
  left_join(all_doy, by = "id") %>%
  filter(!is.na(doy)) %>%
  mutate(geometry = paste0("c(", lon, ", ", lat, ")"))

# List of variable names and their corresponding filenames
files <- c("tmax_monthly_all_tree.rds", 
           "tmin_monthly_all_tree.rds", 
           "prcp_monthly_all_tree.rds",
           "srad_monthly_all_tree.rds")
base_path <- "~/phenology-urban/data/raw/"
processed_data_list <- lapply(files, function(file_name) {
  # Read the file
  var_name <- sub("_monthly_all_tree.rds", "", file_name)
  data <- readRDS(paste0(base_path, city, "/Daymet/monthly2016-2024/", file_name)) %>%
    select(id, value, date) %>%
    mutate(
      season = case_when(
        substr(date, 6, 7) %in% c("03", "04", "05") ~ "spring",
        substr(date, 6, 7) %in% c("06", "07", "08") ~ "summer",
        substr(date, 6, 7) %in% c("09", "10", "11") ~ "fall",
        substr(date, 6, 7) %in% c("12", "01", "02") ~ "winter"
      )) %>%
    mutate(year = as.integer(substr(date, 1, 4)),
           year = if_else(substr(date, 6, 7) == "12", year + 1, year)) %>%
    group_by(id, year, season) %>%
    summarise(
    # Use sum for prcp, and mean for tmax and tmin
    Avg_value = ifelse(var_name == "prcp", sum(value, na.rm = TRUE), mean(value, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  # Rename the Avg_value column to the variable name (e.g., tmax, tmin, prcp)
  rename(!!var_name := Avg_value)
  
  return(data)
})

all_sites_temp <- processed_data_list[[1]]
for (i in 2:length(processed_data_list)) {
  all_sites_temp <- left_join(all_sites_temp, processed_data_list[[i]], by = c("id", "season", "year"))
}

srad_daily <- all_sites_temp %>%
  select(id, year, season, srad) %>%
  rename(Avg_srad = srad)
```

## Discussion

This document records the differences between climate datasets and the potential phenological responses to temperature when using different climate data sources. To further evaluate the suitability of each dataset and inform future data selection, I summarize the key characteristics of both datasets as follows:

-   **Daymet** data: Daymet tends to report slightly lower temperatures and a narrower range of variation compared to WU data, with fewer extreme outliers. It has finer spatial resolution (1 km²) and uniform spatial coverage across the study area.

-   **Weather Underground (WU)** data: WU data generally report slightly higher temperatures and a broader range of variation than Daymet, with more extreme outliers, likely due to less standardized measurement practices of personal weather stations. The data may be limited by the number of available stations, especially in smaller cities, and their uneven spatial distribution. Further analyses require defining a buffer around stations to select relevant trees.
